questions.q: In `ps aux` output, what does the STAT column tell you?
options: The percentage of memory the process is using
How many child processes it has spawned
The process's priority number
The process's current state, such as sleeping (S) or running (R)
questions.explain: STAT shows the process's current state code, like S for sleeping, R for running, or Sl for a sleeping multi-threaded process.

questions.q: You background a job with `./sync-worker.js &` and then close the terminal. What happens to the job?
options: It pauses until you open a new terminal and run `fg`
It receives SIGHUP and typically terminates along with the session
It automatically restarts in a new terminal
It keeps running normally, unaffected by the terminal closing
questions.explain: A background job is still tied to its parent terminal session. Closing the terminal sends SIGHUP, which usually kills the job unless it was started with nohup or similar.

questions.q: What is the key difference between SIGTERM and SIGKILL?
options: SIGKILL only works on root-owned processes
SIGTERM is for background jobs only; SIGKILL is for foreground jobs only
They are two names for the exact same signal
SIGTERM is catchable, letting a process clean up before exiting; SIGKILL is uncatchable and forces immediate termination
questions.explain: SIGTERM (15) asks a process to shut down gracefully and can be intercepted. SIGKILL (9) cannot be caught, ignored, or blocked — the kernel ends the process immediately.

questions.q: Why should you generally try `kill -TERM` before `kill -9` on a misbehaving process?
options: SIGTERM lets the process close files and clean up; SIGKILL gives it no chance to do so, which can leave things in a bad state
kill -9 doesn't actually exist on most systems
They have identical effects, so it doesn't matter
SIGTERM is faster to execute
questions.explain: A clean SIGTERM shutdown lets a process release resources and finish any in-progress work. SIGKILL skips all of that, which can corrupt data or leave lock files behind.

options: Searches log files for the word sync-worker
Lists the PID and full command line of processes whose name matches sync-worker
Starts a new process named sync-worker
Kills every process whose name matches sync-worker
questions.explain: pgrep searches running processes by name and reports matching PIDs; -a additionally shows the full command line for each match. pkill is the equivalent command that sends a signal instead of just listing.
